name: Bexarotene

lead: Bexarotene (Targretin) is a prescription retinoid taken as a capsule or applied as a gel. It is approved for the skin lesions of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
In trials, about half of people with early-stage disease responded, with plaques becoming flatter and clearer.

paras: It activates retinoid X receptors, which partner with other nuclear receptors to regulate cell growth and differentiation.
Common effects are high triglycerides and cholesterol, central hypothyroidism and headache. The label has a boxed warning for birth defects. It is Rx-only.

angle.text: Bexarotene is prescribed to improve skin lesions of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Trials reported reduced plaque elevation, and a small psoriasis study found improved severity with oral use.

lead: Bexarotene (brand name Targretin; development code LGD-1069) is a retinoid that selectively activates retinoid X receptors (RXRs) rather than the retinoic acid receptors targeted by most skin retinoids. It is FDA-approved, as an oral capsule and a topical gel, for the skin manifestations of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), where the visible goal of treatment is flatter, clearer skin plaques.[1][2][3]

Its appearance relevance is tied to that medical setting. In trials of oral bexarotene, a little over half of people with early-stage CTCL and a little under half of those with advanced-stage disease had a measurable response in their skin lesions, and a small psoriasis study reported reduced plaque elevation and severity.[2][4] Because it belongs to the retinoid family, it is sometimes mentioned in skin-focused discussions alongside tretinoin and isotretinoin, but it is a prescription cancer drug with a distinct receptor profile and side-effect pattern.[1]

The US label carries a boxed warning for birth defects, and common effects include raised blood lipids and central hypothyroidism, so treatment involves regular laboratory monitoring.[1][2] Beyond lymphoma, bexarotene has been studied in lung, breast and other cancers, in schizophrenia, and, after a widely publicised 2012 mouse study, in Alzheimer's disease models.[5][6][7][8]
infobox: Rx-only; boxed warning for birth defects

paras: The oral capsule is indicated for the cutaneous manifestations of CTCL in patients refractory to at least one prior systemic therapy.[1] A 1% topical gel was cleared in 2000 for skin lesions of early-stage CTCL.[9] Mycosis fungoides, which makes up roughly 60% of CTCL diagnoses and progresses from patches to plaques to tumours, may be treated with oral bexarotene after skin-directed therapies such as topical steroids and phototherapy.[10] In Europe the oral drug is authorised for advanced-stage disease.[11]

In CTCL, the endpoints that matter visually are the extent and thickness of plaques and patches. Trials graded response by the proportion of lesion area and elevation improved, so responses are described as a lesion-by-lesion clearing or flattening of skin involvement.[2][4] Bexarotene has also been tried for lymphomatoid papulosis, a related chronic papular skin condition, in a small clinical report.[11]

In refractory or persistent early-stage CTCL, the overall response rate was 54% with oral bexarotene; in refractory advanced-stage disease it was 45%.[2] The early-stage results come from a phase II-III trial published in Archives of Dermatology in 2001, and the advanced-stage results from a separate multinational phase II-III study of 94 patients with biopsy-confirmed disease.[4][12]

Topical bexarotene produced response rates of 44% to 63% in early-stage CTCL in separate trials, with the 1% gel applied once to several times daily depending on the study.[2] In psoriasis, oral bexarotene reduced plaque elevation and substantially lowered severity of moderate-to-severe disease in a trial summarised in a review.[2]

In the phase III ALCANZA trial, physician's choice of methotrexate or bexarotene was the comparator against brentuximab vedotin in previously treated CD30-expressing mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma. Final data reported objective responses lasting at least four months in 54.7% of the brentuximab arm and 12.5% of the physician's-choice arm.[13] A real-world analysis and a quality-of-life analysis of the same patient population have also been published.[11]

Outside lymphoma, registered trials have examined bexarotene with chemotherapy in non-small-cell lung cancer (a phase III study enrolling 623 people), in metastatic and at-risk breast cancer, in acute myeloid leukemia, and as an add-on to antipsychotic treatment in chronic schizophrenia (a 90-person phase III registration).[5][6]

The most common adverse events with oral bexarotene are elevated triglycerides and cholesterol, central hypothyroidism and headache; reversible pancreatitis has been reported.[2] Bexarotene suppresses thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine, and it is listed among the drugs that cause central hypothyroidism.[14] Other reported effects include skin dryness and itching, low white blood cell counts and weakness.[11]

The label lists hyperlipidemia, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, hypothyroidism, neutropenia and cataracts as warnings, and describes a hazard with vitamin A supplementation and a hypoglycemia risk in people taking diabetes medicines.[1] Prescribing guidance calls for baseline and ongoing lipid and thyroid monitoring, with dose reduction, interruption or lipid-lowering and thyroid-replacement therapy used to manage changes.[1]

Like other retinoids, bexarotene is contraindicated in pregnancy. The boxed warning states that it is associated with birth defects in humans and caused them in rats and must not be given to a pregnant woman.[1]

Bexarotene binds RXR alpha, beta and gamma. RXRs pair with partner receptors including retinoic acid receptors, the vitamin D receptor, thyroid receptor and PPARs, and the activated complexes regulate genes controlling differentiation, proliferation and apoptosis.[1][2] The exact mechanism of its effect in CTCL is not fully established; it inhibits growth of some hematopoietic and squamous tumour cell lines in vitro.[1][11] Its RXR selectivity distinguishes it from all-trans retinoic acid, which acts mainly on retinoic acid receptors.[11]

Grokipedia and the Wikipedia article on bexarotene describe oral absorption as fairly rapid with a half-life of about 7 hours, more than 99% protein binding and metabolism largely by the liver enzyme CYP3A4.[11][15] The topical gel is applied directly to lesions, which limits systemic exposure compared with the capsule.[3]

Bexarotene was developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals, with patent filings involving SRI International and the La Jolla Cancer Research Foundation.[15] LGD-1069 was the first RXR-selective retinoid to enter clinical trials.[9] Ligand filed the new drug application for the capsules in June 1999 and for the topical gel in December 1999; the FDA approved the capsules at the end of December 1999 and they launched in the US in January 2000.[9] The European Medicines Agency authorised the oral drug in March 2001.[15] Eisai acquired the rights in 2006, US patents expired in 2016, and generic bexarotene is now available.[15]

Bexarotene is prescription-only in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union and Australia.[15] Brand names include Targretin.[1] Online discussion of bexarotene in appearance circles is sparse; where it appears, it is discussed as one of the retinoid-class drugs rather than as a compound used for cosmetic purposes.

In 2012, a paper in Science reported that oral bexarotene rapidly cleared soluble beta-amyloid and reversed deficits in Alzheimer's mouse models by raising apolipoprotein E expression through RXR partner receptors.[7] The result attracted wide attention, and follow-up studies, including published comments in Science, gave mixed results.[15] A later study reported that bexarotene suppressed the primary nucleation step of toxic Aβ42 aggregation in a test-tube system.[8]

A University of Cambridge multiple sclerosis study (CCMR-One) examined bexarotene's ability to promote remyelination, consistent with an earlier report that RXR activation reverses age-related deficits in myelin debris clearance and remyelination in animals.[16][15]
